frameworks.name: Seven Time-Buying Investments
frameworks.definition: A sequenced set of seven outsourcing decisions (meals, laundry, house cleaning, sleep optimization, landscaping, transportation, semi-private flying) ordered by cost-efficiency and number of hours reclaimed per dollar spent.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that the average American spends 13.5 hours per week on meal-related activities (grocery shopping, meal planning, cooking, cleaning, portioning), making food outsourcing the highest-volume time-recovery purchase available to early-stage founders earning more than $16 per hour.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: earner making more than $16 per hour
founder or entrepreneur stage (early)
claims.mechanism: The cost of outsourced meals (~$16/hour equivalent) is below the founder's effective hourly rate, so every hour reclaimed is arbitraged for a net gain; mental bandwidth freed from meal planning also compounds into higher-quality decisions.

numbers.axis: weekly hours spent on meal-related tasks

bounded_by: People who derive genuine value or purpose from cooking may rationally skip this
Applies only while the founder is in income-growth mode; not prescribed for all life stages

claims.text: Alex Hormozi estimates the monthly cost of two outsourced meals per day (shake + lunch + dinner via meal-delivery service) at approximately $750/month, which he frames as net-neutral or net-positive once grocery spending is eliminated and time is monetized at the founder's hourly rate.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: two meals per day outsourced (lunch + dinner; breakfast replaced by shake)
no separate grocery spend maintained
claims.mechanism: Eliminating grocery bills offsets a portion of the meal-delivery cost; the remainder is justified by the time arbitrage at the founder's hourly rate.

anchors.model: alternative: eating same restaurant twice daily (Hormozi's personal approach)
anchors.cost: varies; his Chipotle habit ran ~500+ transactions over multiple years

bounded_by: Does not apply if founder strongly prefers cooking or has dietary restrictions requiring custom preparation

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that the average American spends four hours per week on laundry-related activities (sorting, washing, drying, folding, and putting away clothes), and that outsourcing via drop-off laundry service costs $60 to $80 per month for most people, yielding 16 reclaimed hours per month.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: average American household laundry load (30-40 lbs per month)
bounded_by: People who genuinely enjoy laundry may rationally skip
Cost scales with wardrobe size; fashion-intensive individuals spend significantly more

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that house cleaning (deep clean plus daily tidying) consumes approximately six to seven hours per week for the average person, and that outsourcing it costs $200 to $300 per month, reclaiming roughly 26 hours of monthly time for anyone earning more than $20 per hour.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: earner making more than $20 per hour
standard residential home or apartment
bounded_by: People who enjoy cleaning may rationally skip
Does not account for studio apartments or minimalist living situations with substantially lower cleaning time

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that sleep environment optimization (blackout curtains, earplugs, temperature-regulated mattress) produces more productivity-per-hour rather than more hours, and that the incremental productivity gain from two additional high-quality productive hours per day is equivalent in value to generating two extra hours of clock time.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: applies to knowledge workers and founders in decision-intensive roles
most impactful for people currently sleeping in suboptimal environments (noise, light, temperature)
claims.mechanism: Sleep clears metabolic waste from the brain; insufficient REM sleep accumulates waste that degrades decision quality, focus, and energy; optimizing sleep environment increases REM quality and thereby hourly cognitive output.
bounded_by: Gain is productivity-per-hour, not additional clock hours; not applicable when total hours is the binding constraint

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that outsourcing landscaping and lawn care saves approximately one to two hours per week (mowing) plus two hours per month (weeds/trimming) plus minor gutter time, totaling roughly eight hours per month, at a cost of approximately $300 per month.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: property owner with lawn and landscaping
estimate is per month, averaged across seasonal variation

numbers.axis: hours saved and monthly cost for landscaping outsourcing

bounded_by: Seasonal: mowing time drops to zero in winter climates
Apartment dwellers with no outdoor space should skip

claims.text: Alex Hormozi contends that the average person spends 1.5 hours per day (approximately 30 to 45 hours per month) in commute and transportation, and that replacing personal driving with ride-share or hired drivers costs $600 to $1,000 per month, but only makes economic sense for earners making more than $50 per hour.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: earner making more than $50 per hour
commutes regularly (business travel or daily work commute)
lives in area with reliable ride-share infrastructure
claims.mechanism: Replacing driving with ride-share converts passive commute time into productive work time (tweeting, Slack, project management), effectively doubling the value of each commute hour at the cost of the ride-share fee.
bounded_by: Not applicable in areas without ride-share coverage
Does not apply to people who use commute time for decompression or podcasts they value; the gain is only realized if the reclaimed time is used productively

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that semi-private or charter air travel (e.g., JSX or similar services) saves roughly one to ten hours per trip versus commercial flying by eliminating TSA security, boarding queues, and parking, and that this converts what would be a full travel day into productive work time, at a cost of roughly triple the cheapest commercial fare.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: applies to earners who travel 50-100+ air hours per year
only justified once other lower-cost time-recovery purchases are already in place
additional cost is roughly $1,000/month above baseline travel spend for regular travelers
claims.mechanism: Semi-private eliminates TSA, parking, and boarding queues; the traveler arrives at the plane and boards directly, converting an all-day travel experience into a drive-and-fly sequence and restoring the remaining day to productive work.
bounded_by: Only applies to people who travel regularly; infrequent travelers cannot amortize the cost
Routes and availability limited compared to commercial carriers

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that the full seven-investment stack (meals, laundry, cleaning, sleep optimization, landscaping, transportation, semi-private travel) reclaims approximately 45 hours per week for a total monthly cost of roughly $3,100, and that for non-travelers the same stack minus semi-private flying costs approximately $2,000 per month for approximately 35 hours per week reclaimed.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: earner making $50+ per hour for full stack
earner making $16-50 per hour for partial stacks (meals, laundry, cleaning, sleep)

numbers.axis: cumulative hours reclaimed and monthly cost across all seven investments

bounded_by: Cost and hour estimates are averages; individual variation is substantial based on city, lifestyle, and travel frequency
All estimates are US-based and in 2024 dollars

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that investing in time-reclamation purchases (outsourcing humaning tasks) produces a higher return than S&P 500 investing for founders in income-growth mode, because reclaimed time deployed toward active income growth compounds faster than passive index returns.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: founder in active income-growth mode
reclaimed time is actually deployed toward higher-value productive work, not leisure
founder earns a rate that makes the time-buy arbitrage positive
claims.mechanism: Active income compounds through skill acquisition and business growth at rates substantially above the S&P 500's ~10% annual average; spending $1,000/month to reclaim 20+ hours that generate active income at $50+/hour yields returns an order of magnitude above passive investing.
bounded_by: Does not apply to founders who lack the discipline to deploy reclaimed time productively
Does not apply to retired or passive-income-stage individuals for whom the calculus reverses

claims.text: Alex Hormozi frames 'humaning' (eating, cleaning, laundering, commuting) as the primary structural tax on a founder's productive time, arguing that a founder who outsources all humaning effectively has two weeks for every one calendar week that non-outsourcing peers have.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: founder earning above the per-task arbitrage thresholds ($16-$50+/hour depending on category)
reclaimed hours used for high-value work
claims.mechanism: A standard 16-hour waking day loses 4-6 hours to humaning tasks for the average person; outsourcing those tasks restores those hours to productive use, effectively creating a second work week inside the same calendar week.

numbers.axis: productive hours available per waking day

anchors.productive_hours: ~10-12 of 16 waking hours (4-6 lost to humaning)

bounded_by: Gain is only realized if reclaimed time is used for income-productive or skill-building activities
Some humaning tasks (cooking, if it provides genuine recovery or creative value) may legitimately not be outsourced

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that time-reclamation investments are one-time-purchase decisions with compounding lifetime value: the hours bought back cannot be repurchased retroactively, so the opportunity cost of delaying these investments is permanently lost productive time.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: applies to founders in active earning and growth seasons of their career
claims.mechanism: Productive career seasons are finite; time spent on low-value tasks during high-earnings years cannot be recouped. Unlike a stock purchase that can be made later at a similar return profile, productive hours are non-renewable once the season passes.
bounded_by: Less applicable to people with unlimited career runway or who are not yet earning above the arbitrage thresholds
Does not apply to tasks the individual derives intrinsic meaning from

examples.text: Alex Hormozi ate at Chipotle twice a day for multiple years, accumulating over 500 Chipotle transactions according to his accountant. He frames this as systematic meal outsourcing: his grocery bills were effectively zero (only Red Bull and Coke Zero), freeing all grocery, planning, cooking, cleaning, and portioning time. His accountant challenged the spending; Hormozi's rebuttal was that the time savings and cognitive bandwidth freed by the consistency justified the cost, especially compared to the near-zero grocery bill.

Hormozi describes sitting outside laundromats working on laptops with his wife Layla during a period when they were traveling frequently across the country. Because they moved so often, finding a consistent drop-off laundry service was difficult, so the laundromat (do all loads at once and leave) was more efficient than stringing out laundry over a full day at home. He uses this as a secondary endorsement of the laundromat model for anyone who currently spends an entire day cycling through wash-fold-dry at home.

Hormozi describes his personal workaround for apartment cleaning before he hired cleaners: he simply did not touch anything, reasoning that if nothing got dirty, nothing needed to be cleaned. He frames this as an improvised version of outsourcing (zero inputs = zero cleaning requirement), while acknowledging it is not a scalable solution for most founders.

Hormozi describes tracking sleep via a sleep-tracking mattress and noticing that watching TV or using a phone before bed pushes REM sleep backward in the night, reducing its quality. He explains the mechanism: the brain uses sleep to clear metabolic waste; insufficient or low-quality sleep leaves this waste uncleared, producing the feeling of having 'no juice in the middle of my brain.' He uses this as his personal example of why sleep environment optimization (blackout curtains, earplugs, cooling mattress) is non-negotiable for him in Las Vegas.

Hormozi compares a Las Vegas-to-Los Angeles commercial flight (Spirit at ~$50-99), a semi-private JSX flight (~$300), and a full private charter (~$15,000-20,000). He notes the JSX experience is 'so close to what you get in private for such a fraction of the price,' and that what would otherwise be a full travel day (check-in, TSA, gate wait, boarding) becomes a drive-to-plane-and-work sequence. He frames JSX as accessible to founders who travel regularly but cannot justify full private.

Hormozi describes his uniform simplification practice: one shelf of white tank tops (wife beaters) and one shelf of black shorts, selected without thinking in the dark. He frames this as a micro-version of the same outsourcing principle applied to decision-making: reducing the number of daily micro-decisions frees cognitive bandwidth for higher-value choices. The example illustrates that the principle extends beyond paid outsourcing to any friction elimination that reclaims mental bandwidth.

practices.text: Start with meal outsourcing first before laundry, cleaning, or other categories, because meals check the most boxes simultaneously (time reclaimed, cognitive bandwidth freed, potential weight loss or body composition improvement from controlled portions).

Treat sleep environment optimization as a zero-priority item (assign it cost rank zero in the stack) because the one-time cost is minimal and the productivity-per-hour improvement is permanent; do it before spending on landscaping or transportation.

Use electrical tape on small indicator lights in the bedroom (router LEDs, power strips, etc.) to eliminate all light sources without damaging paint; combine with blackout curtains and earplugs as a low-cost sleep environment baseline.
Wear the same clothing style every day (uniform dress) to eliminate morning decision friction and save cognitive bandwidth for higher-value choices.

Use productive ride-share time for high-leverage activities such as social media posting, Slack message processing, or project status updates rather than passive consumption, to fully monetize the reclaimed commute time.
